diagnoses: Drug Rash with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 42-year-old female presents with 3 weeks of tiredness and nausea.
hints: Vomiting since yesterday. Vague generalised abdominal pain. No diarrhoea.
5 kg weight loss. Light-headed on standing. Craving salty food.
PMH: vitiligo, hypothyroidism on levothyroxine. Recent flu-like illness.
O/E: BP 88/54 lying, 66/40 standing. Pigmented palmar creases and buccal mucosa.
Na 122, K 6.2, glucose 2.9, urea 11.4. 9am cortisol 48 nmol/L.
puzzles.explanation: Acute adrenal insufficiency. Autoimmune adrenalitis is the commonest UK cause and clusters with other autoimmune disease. Hyperpigmentation reflects high ACTH; an intercurrent illness tips chronic insufficiency into crisis.
puzzles.management: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately, IV 0.9% saline, treat the precipitant, correct hypoglycaemia. Do not delay steroids for the Short Synacthen test. Steroid card and sick-day rules on discharge.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Addison's disease

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 63-year-old male presents after collapsing in the garden.
hints: Brief loss of consciousness, alert on arrival. Vague ache between the shoulder blades.
Ache began abruptly and was worst at onset. Now settling. Feels 'not right'.
PMH: hypertension, poorly controlled. 40 pack-year smoker. Tall with long arm span.
O/E: BP 176/94 right arm, 132/76 left arm. Early diastolic murmur at left sternal edge.
ECG: sinus rhythm, no ST change. Troponin normal. CXR: widened mediastinum.
puzzles.explanation: A tear in the aortic intima lets blood track through the media. Pain is often maximal at onset then eases, which falsely reassures. Interarm BP difference, a new aortic regurgitation murmur and syncope point to a type A dissection.
puzzles.management: CT angiogram aorta. Cautious BP and heart-rate control with IV beta-blockade (target systolic 100–120). Type A: emergency cardiothoracic surgery. Type B: usually medical unless complicated. Avoid anticoagulation.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Aortic dissection

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 71-year-old female presents with 5 weeks of headache and feeling run down.
hints: Dull right-sided head pain. Paracetamol has made no difference.
Aching and stiffness in both shoulders, worst first thing in the morning.
Scalp sore when brushing her hair. Jaw aches after a few minutes of chewing.
Vision in the right eye greyed out yesterday for 2 minutes, then recovered.
O/E: thickened, tender, pulseless right temporal artery. ESR 96, CRP 88.
puzzles.explanation: Large-vessel vasculitis of the extracranial branches of the carotid. Jaw claudication and scalp tenderness are the most specific features; amaurosis fugax warns of impending anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, which causes irreversible blindness. Overlaps with polymyalgia rheumatica.
puzzles.management: Start high-dose glucocorticoid immediately on clinical suspicion — do not wait for biopsy. Prednisolone 40–60 mg daily, or IV methylprednisolone if visual symptoms. Same-day ophthalmology if any visual loss. Temporal artery biopsy within 2 weeks; bone and gastric protection.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Giant cell arteritis

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 34-year-old male presents with low back pain after lifting a heavy box.
hints: Pain now runs down both legs. Legs feel heavy going up stairs.
Had to strain to start passing urine this morning. Then wet himself once.
Odd numbness when wiping after opening his bowels.
O/E: reduced sensation over the perineum and inner thighs. Reduced anal tone on PR.
Ankle reflexes absent bilaterally. Bladder scan: 940 ml residual volume.
puzzles.explanation: Compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus, usually by a large central disc prolapse. Painless retention with overflow incontinence and saddle anaesthesia are the red flags; delay risks permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction.
puzzles.management: Emergency whole-spine MRI, same day. Immediate spinal surgical referral — do not wait for the scan to refer. Surgical decompression, ideally within 48 hours of onset and sooner if incomplete.
puzzles.source: NICE NG59 – Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 24-year-old female presents with 2 days of dizziness and loose stools.
hints: Crampy lower abdominal pain, worse on the left. Feels faint on standing.
Ache at the tip of the left shoulder, worse when lying flat.
Periods usually regular; last one 7 weeks ago and lighter than normal.
PMH: chlamydia treated aged 20. Copper coil in situ.
HR 118, BP 92/58. Urine hCG positive. TVUS: empty uterus, 3 cm left adnexal mass, free fluid in the pouch of Douglas.
puzzles.explanation: Implantation outside the uterine cavity, most often in the fallopian tube. GI upset, shoulder-tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation and dizziness can dominate before any bleeding. Prior PID and an IUD raise the risk. Pregnancy test every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain.
puzzles.management: A-E assessment with large-bore IV access, group and save, cross-match. Urgent gynaecology referral. Haemodynamic instability or rupture: emergency laparoscopic salpingectomy. Stable and small with low hCG: methotrexate or expectant management via an early pregnancy unit.
puzzles.source: NICE NG126 – Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 34-year-old female presents with 3 days of feeling light-headed.
hints: Breathless going upstairs, which is new for her. Dry cough. No fever.
Sharp right-sided chest pain, only when she breathes in deeply.
Right calf has felt tight for a week. Started the combined pill 4 months ago.
O/E: RR 24, HR 112, sats 93% on air. Chest clear. Right calf 3 cm larger.
ECG: sinus tachycardia. CXR normal. CTPA: filling defect in the right lower lobe artery.
puzzles.explanation: Thrombus, usually from a deep leg vein, lodging in the pulmonary arteries. Presentation is often vague — dizziness, mild breathlessness, an unexplained tachycardia — rather than dramatic. Oestrogen-containing contraception is a common and easily missed risk factor in young women.
puzzles.management: Wells score, then CTPA (or V/Q if renal impairment or pregnancy). Start therapeutic anticoagulation, usually a DOAC, before imaging if delay is likely. Thrombolysis only for haemodynamic instability. Stop the combined pill and review contraception.
puzzles.source: NICE NG158 – Venous thromboembolic diseases

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 17-year-old male presents with 2 days of abdominal pain and vomiting.
hints: No diarrhoea. Abdomen generally sore, soft, no guarding.
6 kg weight loss in a month. Drinking constantly, up three times a night to pass urine.
PMH: nil. Sister has coeliac disease. Flu-like illness last week.
O/E: dry mucous membranes, deep sighing respiration at 28/min. Sweet smell on the breath.
Glucose 31, ketones 5.8, pH 7.12, bicarbonate 9, K 5.4.
puzzles.explanation: Insulin deficiency drives ketogenesis and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Abdominal pain and vomiting can dominate and mimic a surgical abdomen; a new type 1 diabetic often presents this way after an intercurrent illness. Kussmaul breathing is the acidosis, not a chest problem.
puzzles.management: Fixed-rate IV insulin infusion (0.1 units/kg/hr) plus 0.9% saline. Continue long-acting insulin. Replace potassium once below 5.5 — it will fall fast. Hourly ketones, glucose and VBG. Add 10% glucose when glucose drops below 14.
puzzles.source: JBDS / NICE NG17 – Type 1 diabetes in adults

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 74-year-old female presents with confusion since this morning.
hints: Shivering episodes overnight, teeth chattering under two blankets.
Off her food for 3 days. Vague discomfort under the right ribs.
Daughter thinks her eyes look yellow. Urine darker than usual.
O/E: Temp 38.9, HR 116, BP 86/52. Tender right upper quadrant. Jaundiced sclerae.
Bilirubin 96, ALP 480, ALT 110, WCC 19, CRP 240. USS: dilated common bile duct with a stone.
puzzles.explanation: Bacterial infection of an obstructed biliary tree. Charcot's triad is fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain; adding confusion and hypotension makes Reynolds' pentad and signals a septic emergency. Older patients often present with confusion alone.
puzzles.management: Sepsis six with blood cultures and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics. Fluid resuscitation. Urgent biliary decompression by ERCP, ideally within 24 hours, or percutaneous drainage if ERCP is not possible. Interval cholecystectomy.
puzzles.source: NICE CG188 – Gallstone disease

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 58-year-old male presents with a painful left lower leg.
hints: Scratched it on a garden fence 2 days ago. Says it feels far worse than it looks.
Needing regular morphine and still rates the pain 10/10. Spreading since this morning.
PMH: type 2 diabetes on metformin. BMI 38.
O/E: dusky violet patch with a blister. Skin numb over it. Crackling under the fingers.
Temp 39.1, HR 128, BP 90/50. WCC 24, CRP 310, lactate 4.8, Na 128, creatinine 180.
puzzles.explanation: Rapidly spreading infection of the deep fascia. Pain out of proportion to visible skin change is the earliest and most important sign; anaesthesia over the area, dusky discolouration and crepitus are late. Diabetes and obesity are major risk factors. It is a clinical diagnosis — imaging must not delay theatre.
puzzles.management: Immediate surgical referral for urgent radical debridement — this is the only definitive treatment. Sepsis six, aggressive fluid resuscitation, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics with clindamycin for toxin suppression. Critical care involvement. Expect repeat debridement.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Cellulitis and erysipelas

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 66-year-old female presents with a headache and vomiting.
hints: Started this evening while she was at the cinema. Right-sided and severe.
Vision blurred on that side. Halos around the streetlights on the way home.
PMH: long-sighted since childhood. Started an antihistamine for hay fever yesterday.
O/E: right eye red, cornea hazy. Pupil mid-dilated and unreactive.
Globe feels hard. Intraocular pressure 54 mmHg right, 16 mmHg left.
puzzles.explanation: The peripheral iris blocks the trabecular meshwork and intraocular pressure rises sharply. Headache and vomiting can eclipse the eye symptoms entirely and get mistaken for migraine or gastroenteritis. Precipitated by pupil dilation — dim light, or anticholinergic drugs. Hypermetropes have shallower anterior chambers and are at higher risk.
puzzles.management: Emergency same-day ophthalmology referral. Lie the patient flat. IV acetazolamide plus topical pilocarpine, beta-blocker and steroid to lower pressure. Definitive treatment is bilateral laser peripheral iridotomy — the fellow eye is also at risk.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Glaucoma

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 14-year-old male presents with lower abdominal pain and vomiting.
hints: Came on suddenly during football 3 hours ago. No fever.
No dysuria or frequency. Bowels normal. Appendicectomy scar absent.
Two similar episodes in the past year that settled on their own within an hour.
O/E: abdomen soft. On exposure the left hemiscrotum is swollen; testis sits high and transverse.
Cremasteric reflex absent on the left. Elevating the testis makes the pain worse.
puzzles.explanation: The spermatic cord twists and cuts off testicular blood supply. Adolescents very often present complaining only of abdominal pain and vomiting, so the scrotum must be examined in every boy with abdominal pain. Prior self-resolving episodes suggest intermittent torsion. Salvage falls sharply after 6 hours.
puzzles.management: Immediate urology referral for scrotal exploration — do not delay for a Doppler ultrasound. Nil by mouth, analgesia. Bilateral orchidopexy at surgery, since the bell-clapper deformity is usually bilateral. Orchidectomy if the testis is non-viable.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Scrotal pain and swelling

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 29-year-old female presents with 3 weeks of headaches and poor concentration.
hints: Nausea most mornings. Pregnancy test negative. Sleeping badly.
Headache clears a few hours after she gets to work, and is worst at weekends.
Moved into a rented flat 2 months ago. Her flatmate has the same symptoms.
The cat has been off its food and seems unsteady.
Old gas boiler in the kitchen, no alarm fitted. O/E: normal neurology, sats 99%. COHb 19%.
puzzles.explanation: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with far greater affinity than oxygen and shifts the dissociation curve left. Symptoms are non-specific and routinely mistaken for viral illness or depression. The clue is the pattern: better away from the building, worse at home, and other occupants or pets affected. Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal.
puzzles.management: Remove from exposure and give high-flow oxygen via non-rebreathe mask until COHb is below 3%. Measure COHb on a venous or arterial sample. Consider hyperbaric oxygen for loss of consciousness, neurological signs, pregnancy or COHb above 20%. Report to environmental health and stop the household returning.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Carbon monoxide poisoning

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 78-year-old male brought in by his daughter, gradually more muddled over 6 weeks.
hints: Sleeping more than usual. Daughter says he is not himself. No fever.
Dull constant headache. Unsteady on his feet, two near-falls this month.
PMH: atrial fibrillation on apixaban. Tripped on a kerb 2 months ago, no scan at the time.
O/E: AMTS 6/10. Subtle left pronator drift. Pupils equal and reactive.
CT head: crescentic hypodense collection over the right convexity with 12 mm midline shift.
puzzles.explanation: Bridging veins tear and bleed slowly into the subdural space. Cerebral atrophy and anticoagulation make older patients vulnerable, and the head injury is often trivial or forgotten. The picture is insidious cognitive decline, so it is frequently mislabelled as dementia or delirium. The collection crosses suture lines and is crescent-shaped, unlike an extradural.
puzzles.management: Urgent CT head and neurosurgical referral. Reverse anticoagulation and review the indication. Burr hole drainage for a symptomatic collection with mass effect. Conservative management with repeat imaging if small and asymptomatic. Falls assessment before discharge.
puzzles.source: NICE NG232 – Head injury: assessment and early management

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 69-year-old male presents with 4 months of back pain and constipation.
hints: Mid-back pain, worse at night, no injury. Paracetamol is not helping.
Exhausted all the time. Thirsty and passing more urine than usual.
Three chest infections since Christmas. 7 kg weight loss.
Hb 92 with normal MCV, ESR 110, calcium 3.1, creatinine 168, albumin 30.
Blood film shows rouleaux. Serum electrophoresis: IgG paraprotein band. Spine X-ray: T9 wedge fracture.
puzzles.explanation: Clonal plasma cell proliferation producing a paraprotein. Remember CRAB: hyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lesions. The constipation, thirst and confusion here are hypercalcaemia, not a bowel problem, and recurrent infection reflects immunoparesis. A very high ESR with normocytic anaemia in an older patient with back pain should prompt the test.
puzzles.management: Treat hypercalcaemia with IV 0.9% saline then bisphosphonate. Urgent haematology referral. Serum and urine electrophoresis, serum free light chains, whole-body MRI or low-dose CT. Treatment is combination chemotherapy with autologous stem cell transplant in fitter patients, plus bone protection.
puzzles.source: NICE NG35 – Myeloma: diagnosis and management

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 31-year-old female presents at 34 weeks pregnant with heartburn and a headache.
hints: Burning pain under the ribs since yesterday. Gaviscon has not touched it.
Frontal headache, and occasional flashing lights in her vision.
Rings no longer fit. Face and hands puffy over the last week. First pregnancy.
O/E: BP 168/112 on two readings 20 minutes apart. Three beats of ankle clonus.
Urine dipstick protein 3+. Platelets 88, ALT 140, protein:creatinine ratio 62 mg/mmol.
puzzles.explanation: New hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or organ dysfunction. Epigastric pain is liver capsule stretch, not reflux, and together with visual disturbance, headache and clonus marks severe disease at risk of eclampsia. The deranged platelets and transaminases here indicate HELLP. Nulliparity is a risk factor.
puzzles.management: Admit. Labetalol (or nifedipine) to keep BP below 135/85. IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis and treatment. Senior obstetric review; delivery is the only cure and is the plan at 34 weeks with severe features, after antenatal corticosteroids. Monitor bloods and fluid balance closely.
puzzles.source: NICE NG133 – Hypertension in pregnancy

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 78-year-old female presents with 6 hours of abdominal pain and loose stools.
hints: Vomited twice. Pain is constant and central, not colicky.
Rates the pain 10/10, but lies still and looks comfortable between questions.
PMH: atrial fibrillation, declined anticoagulation 2 years ago. Ex-smoker.
O/E: abdomen soft with minimal tenderness. Bowel sounds present. HR 104, irregular.
Lactate 5.2, WCC 21, pH 7.28. AXR unremarkable. CT angiogram: SMA occlusion.
puzzles.explanation: Embolic or thrombotic occlusion of the mesenteric circulation. The hallmark is pain grossly out of proportion to a soft, unimpressive abdomen, with a normal plain film — so it is repeatedly dismissed as gastroenteritis. Untreated AF is the classic source. Peritonism and a rigid abdomen are late, and mean infarcted bowel.
puzzles.management: Urgent CT angiography — do not wait for peritonism. Aggressive fluid resuscitation, IV antibiotics, analgesia and early surgical referral. Laparotomy for resection of non-viable bowel, with revascularisation by embolectomy or stenting. Mortality is high.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Acute abdominal pain

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 72-year-old male presents with left loin pain and one episode of collapse.
hints: Pain came on abruptly an hour ago and radiates into the left groin.
Went grey and clammy at onset. Vomited once. Restless and cannot get comfortable.
PMH: hypertension, 50 pack-year smoker. Brother had an aneurysm repaired.
O/E: BP 94/58, HR 110. Tender expansile mass above the umbilicus.
Urine dipstick: blood 1+. Bedside ultrasound: 7.4 cm infrarenal aorta with free fluid.
puzzles.explanation: Rupture classically masquerades as renal colic — loin-to-groin pain, restlessness and microscopic haematuria on the dip. First presentation of renal colic over 60 should be assumed to be a leaking aneurysm until proven otherwise. An expansile (not merely pulsatile) mass is the key sign.
puzzles.management: Do not delay for imaging if unstable. Two large-bore cannulae, activate major haemorrhage protocol, permissive hypotension targeting a systolic around 90. Immediate vascular surgical referral for open repair or EVAR. CT angiogram only if stable enough.
puzzles.source: NICE NG156 – Abdominal aortic aneurysm

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 52-year-old male brought in by a friend, unsteady and muddled for 2 days.
hints: Eating very little for several weeks. Vomiting most mornings.
Friend says he is normally sharp; today he cannot recall the date or how he got here.
Drinks around 60 units a week. Last drink 3 days ago.
O/E: wide-based gait, cannot walk heel to toe. Horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze.
Right lateral rectus palsy. Glucose 4.8, no focal weakness, CT head normal.
puzzles.explanation: Acute thiamine deficiency. The triad of confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia is complete in only a minority, so any one feature in a malnourished or alcohol-dependent patient should trigger treatment. Giving glucose before thiamine can precipitate it. Untreated it progresses to irreversible Korsakoff syndrome.
puzzles.management: IV Pabrinex (high-dose B vitamins) immediately, before any glucose-containing fluid. Treat for at least 5 days, then oral thiamine. Manage alcohol withdrawal with a benzodiazepine and a CIWA-based regimen. Correct magnesium, which is needed for thiamine to work.
puzzles.source: NICE CG100 – Alcohol-use disorders: physical complications

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 45-year-old female brought in by her husband, behaving strangely since yesterday.
hints: Husband says she has been saying odd things and got lost driving a familiar route.
Mild headache for 3 days. Felt fluish last week.
Witnessed episode this morning of staring and lip-smacking lasting a minute.
O/E: Temp 38.4, GCS 14. Word-finding difficulty. No neck stiffness, no rash.
CT head normal. CSF: lymphocytes 120, protein 0.9, normal glucose. MRI: temporal lobe change.
puzzles.explanation: Inflammation of the brain parenchyma, most often herpes simplex, which has a predilection for the temporal lobes. Altered behaviour, personality change and dysphasia dominate rather than meningism — so it is easily mistaken for a psychiatric presentation or delirium. Focal seizures are common. Delay in treatment sharply worsens outcome.
puzzles.management: Start IV aciclovir empirically on suspicion — before the CSF result. CT head, then lumbar puncture for viral PCR if no contraindication. MRI is more sensitive than CT. Treat seizures, monitor for raised intracranial pressure, and involve neurology. Continue aciclovir until HSV PCR is negative.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Meningitis and encephalitis

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 64-year-old male presents with 3 weeks of mid-back pain.
hints: Pain is worse lying flat and at night, and wakes him. Worse on coughing.
Legs have felt heavy and unreliable for 4 days. Stumbled twice today.
PMH: prostate cancer on hormone therapy. 5 kg weight loss.
O/E: sensory level at the umbilicus. Increased tone in both legs, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars.
Bladder scan 500 ml. MRI whole spine: T10 metastasis with epidural extension.
puzzles.explanation: Metastatic deposit compressing the cord, most often from breast, lung or prostate primaries. Nocturnal back pain worse on lying flat and on coughing precedes neurology by weeks and is the window for intervention. Upper motor neurone signs with a sensory level distinguish it from cauda equina, which gives flaccid weakness and areflexia.
puzzles.management: Whole-spine MRI within 24 hours. Dexamethasone 16 mg daily with PPI cover, started immediately. Discuss same day with the acute oncology and spinal services. Definitive treatment is radiotherapy or surgical decompression. Flat bed rest with log-rolling until the spine is declared stable. VTE prophylaxis.
puzzles.source: NICE NG234 – Spinal metastases and metastatic spinal cord compression

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 38-year-old female presents agitated and unable to stop vomiting.
hints: Family say she has been anxious and irritable for months and assumed panic attacks.
Diarrhoea for 2 days. Feels unbearably hot and cannot sit still.
8 kg weight loss over 3 months. Chest infection last week treated with antibiotics.
O/E: Temp 39.2, HR 152 irregularly irregular. Fine tremor, warm and sweating. Mild proptosis.
TSH <0.01, free T4 68. ECG: fast atrial fibrillation. LFTs mildly deranged.
puzzles.explanation: Decompensated thyrotoxicosis, usually Graves', tipped over by an intercurrent illness. Agitation, fever, vomiting and tachyarrhythmia are easily attributed to sepsis or a psychiatric crisis, and the thyroid is often not examined. It is a clinical diagnosis — the T4 is not necessarily higher than in uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis.
puzzles.management: Propranolol for adrenergic symptoms, propylthiouracil or carbimazole to block synthesis, then iodine (Lugol's) at least an hour later. IV hydrocortisone. Aggressive fluids, active cooling, treat the precipitant. Critical care input — mortality is significant.
puzzles.source: NICE NG145 – Thyroid disease: assessment and management

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 68-year-old female presents with a swollen, painful right knee.
hints: Came on over 24 hours. Cannot weight bear at all.
She has had gout in the big toe twice before and assumed this was the same.
PMH: rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and adalimumab. Steroid injection to that knee 3 weeks ago.
O/E: Temp 38.1. Knee hot with a tense effusion. Resists any passive movement.
WCC 17, CRP 220. Aspirate: turbid, WCC 78,000, no crystals, Gram-positive cocci.
puzzles.explanation: Bacterial infection of a joint, usually Staphylococcus aureus. Immunosuppression, existing joint disease and recent intra-articular injection are the major risks, and the patient's own gout history is a trap — crystal arthropathy and infection look identical and can coexist. Cartilage is destroyed within days.
puzzles.management: Joint aspiration for urgent Gram stain, culture and crystals BEFORE antibiotics. Blood cultures. IV flucloxacillin (or vancomycin if MRSA risk) for around 2 weeks, then oral to complete 4–6 weeks. Urgent orthopaedic referral for washout. Withhold the biologic and involve rheumatology.
puzzles.source: BSR / NICE CKS – Septic arthritis

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 61-year-old male presents feeling faint and short of breath.
hints: Something 'went' in his upper abdomen an hour ago while he was watching television.
Now sore across the whole abdomen and up into the right shoulder.
Takes ibuprofen most days for knee pain. Occasional indigestion for months.
O/E: lying completely still. Abdomen rigid with board-like guarding, bowel sounds absent.
HR 118, BP 98/60. Erect CXR: free air under both hemidiaphragms. Lactate 3.4, WCC 19.
puzzles.explanation: Full-thickness perforation spilling gastric contents into the peritoneum. Shoulder-tip pain is referred diaphragmatic irritation, and the patient lying rigidly still is generalised peritonitis. NSAID use is the commonest precipitant. Presenting with faintness and breathlessness rather than pain can send the workup down a cardiac route.
puzzles.management: A-E assessment, nil by mouth, NG tube, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, PPI and analgesia. Erect chest X-ray, or CT if equivocal. Urgent surgical referral for laparotomy with omental patch repair and washout. Stop NSAIDs and test for H. pylori afterwards.
puzzles.source: NICE CG184 – Gastro-oesophageal reflux and dyspepsia

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 82-year-old male presents from his care home with abdominal swelling.
hints: No bowel movement for 5 days and not passing wind since yesterday.
Vomited twice this morning. Pain is mild and crampy rather than severe.
PMH: Parkinson's disease, chronic constipation. Similar admission last year that settled.
O/E: abdomen grossly distended and tympanic, but soft with no guarding. Rectum empty on PR.
AXR: massively dilated loop arising from the pelvis with a coffee bean appearance.
puzzles.explanation: The sigmoid twists on its mesentery, causing closed-loop large bowel obstruction. Typical in older, constipated, institutionalised patients, often with neurological disease, and recurrence is common. Gross distension with a soft abdomen is characteristic; pain and tenderness suggest ischaemia or perforation.
puzzles.management: IV fluids, nil by mouth, NG tube. Endoscopic decompression with a flexible sigmoidoscope and flatus tube is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Surgery (sigmoid colectomy) if decompression fails, or if there is ischaemia, perforation or repeated recurrence.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Constipation / ACPGBI large bowel obstruction guidance

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 80-year-old female presents with a week of nausea and poor appetite.
hints: Vomiting on and off. No diarrhoea now. Family say she seems muddled.
Complains the television looks yellow-tinged and blurred.
PMH: atrial fibrillation and heart failure. Amiodarone started 3 weeks ago.
Diarrhoea and vomiting illness last week; has been drinking very little since.
O/E: HR 44 regular. K 5.7, creatinine 190 (baseline 92). ECG: downsloping ST depression.
puzzles.explanation: Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index and is renally cleared, so any AKI raises the level. Amiodarone displaces it and reduces clearance further. Nausea, confusion and xanthopsia (yellow-tinged vision) are classic but easily blamed on age or a viral illness. Hyperkalaemia indicates significant toxicity and predicts mortality.
puzzles.management: Stop digoxin and the interacting drug. Check digoxin level, U&Es and ECG. Treat hyperkalaemia — but avoid calcium in digoxin toxicity. Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia. Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab) for haemodynamic instability, arrhythmia or potassium above 5.5.
puzzles.source: NICE BNF / TOXBASE – Digoxin

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 26-year-old male presents with abdominal cramps and feeling faint after lunch.
hints: Cramps started around 15 minutes after eating. Vomited once. No diarrhoea.
Palms and scalp feel itchy. Says his voice has gone husky.
PMH: asthma, well controlled. Ate a takeaway curry, has eaten there before.
O/E: widespread wheeze. Lips and eyelids swollen. Blotchy raised rash over the trunk.
HR 128, BP 82/44, sats 92% on air, RR 26.
puzzles.explanation: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation. Gastrointestinal symptoms are a recognised feature of food-triggered anaphylaxis and can arrive before or instead of an obvious rash, which delays recognition. Airway, breathing or circulation compromise plus sudden onset after a likely trigger is enough — the rash is not required. Asthma raises the risk of a fatal outcome.
puzzles.management: IM adrenaline 500 micrograms into the anterolateral thigh, repeated after 5 minutes if needed. Remove the trigger, lie flat with legs raised, high-flow oxygen, IV fluid bolus. Adjuncts only after adrenaline. Observe 6–12 hours for a biphasic reaction. Serum tryptase, adrenaline auto-injector and allergy clinic referral.
puzzles.source: Resuscitation Council UK / NICE CG134 – Anaphylaxis

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 13-year-old male presents with 6 weeks of left knee pain.
hints: No injury he can recall. Pain is dull and worse after football.
Mother has noticed him limping and dragging the left leg for a fortnight.
BMI on the 98th centile. Prepubertal for his age.
O/E: knee entirely normal — no effusion, full painless range of movement.
Left hip externally rotates as it is flexed. Frog-leg lateral X-ray: epiphysis slipped posteromedially.
puzzles.explanation: Displacement of the femoral head through the growth plate in an adolescent, typically an overweight boy. Pain is referred to the knee via the obturator nerve in around a quarter of cases, so a normal knee examination is entirely expected — every child with knee pain needs their hips examined. Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion is the classic sign. Delay risks avascular necrosis.
puzzles.management: Non-weight bearing immediately and urgent orthopaedic referral. AP and frog-leg lateral X-rays of both hips. Surgical fixation in situ with a single cannulated screw. Consider prophylactic fixation of the other hip, since bilateral slip is common.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Hip pain in children

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 2-year-old male brought in by his mother, drawing his legs up and crying in spells.
hints: Episodes last a couple of minutes every 20 minutes or so. Between them he is floppy and quiet.
Vomiting since this morning. Milky at first, now green.
Had a cold with a runny nose last week. Fully vaccinated.
O/E: pale and lethargic. Sausage-shaped mass palpable in the right upper quadrant.
Nappy contains dark red jelly-like stool. Ultrasound: target sign in the right abdomen.
puzzles.explanation: One segment of bowel telescopes into the next, usually ileocolic, often after a viral illness has enlarged Peyer's patches. The intermittent colic with lethargy in between is highly characteristic and is often mistaken for colic or gastroenteritis. Redcurrant jelly stool is a late sign — waiting for it means waiting too long.
puzzles.management: IV fluid resuscitation, nil by mouth, NG tube. Ultrasound is diagnostic. Reduction by air enema under radiological guidance if stable and no perforation. Laparotomy if enema fails or there is peritonitis or perforation. Consider a pathological lead point in children over 2.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Abdominal pain in children

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 54-year-old male presents with 6 weeks of night sweats and feeling washed out.
hints: Intermittent low-grade fevers. 6 kg weight loss. Two courses of antibiotics from his GP, no better.
Aching in several joints and in the lower back.
PMH: bicuspid aortic valve. Extensive dental work 2 months ago, no prophylaxis.
O/E: Temp 37.9. New early diastolic murmur. Splinter haemorrhages in two nails. Spleen tip palpable.
Hb 98, CRP 140, urine dip blood 2+. Three sets of blood cultures grow Streptococcus. Echo: aortic vegetation.
puzzles.explanation: Infection of the endocardium, usually on an abnormal or prosthetic valve. It presents as a prolonged non-specific illness — sweats, weight loss, joint pains — and is repeatedly treated as a viral illness or PUO. Microscopic haematuria and a new murmur are the tells. Modified Duke criteria combine blood cultures, echo findings and predisposing factors.
puzzles.management: Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics. Transthoracic then transoesophageal echo. Prolonged IV antibiotics, 4–6 weeks, guided by microbiology. Endocarditis team involvement. Surgery for heart failure, uncontrolled infection, abscess or recurrent emboli.
puzzles.source: NICE CG64 / ESC – Infective endocarditis

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 71-year-old female presents with a numb, weak right leg since this morning.
hints: Came on suddenly while she was sitting down. Cannot wiggle her toes properly.
Aching pain in the calf and foot, constant, not related to walking.
PMH: atrial fibrillation, stopped her anticoagulant last month because of bruising.
O/E: right foot pale and cool to mid-calf. Left foot warm. Speech and face normal.
No palpable popliteal or pedal pulses on the right. Calf tender and firm. No Doppler signal.
puzzles.explanation: Sudden arterial occlusion, usually embolic from AF. Numbness and weakness of a limb triggers an automatic stroke reflex, but the absent pulses, cold pale limb and normal cranial nerves place the lesion in the artery, not the brain. The six Ps are pain, pallor, pulselessness, perishing cold, paraesthesia and paralysis; the last two mean the limb is threatened.
puzzles.management: Immediate vascular surgical referral — irreversible damage within 6 hours. IV heparin infusion, analgesia, nil by mouth, keep the limb dependent and warm. Urgent CT angiography if it does not delay treatment. Embolectomy, thrombolysis or bypass depending on category. Restart long-term anticoagulation.
puzzles.source: NICE CG147 – Peripheral arterial disease

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 39-year-old male presents with 4 days of clumsy, heavy legs.
hints: Started as tingling in both feet, now up to the knees. Struggling on stairs.
Hands starting to feel the same since yesterday. No back pain.
Bad episode of diarrhoea 3 weeks ago that settled on its own.
O/E: symmetrical weakness, worse distally. Reflexes absent throughout. Sensation largely intact.
Forced vital capacity 1.4 L and falling. CSF: protein 1.4, normal cell count.
puzzles.explanation: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, typically triggered by an infection a few weeks earlier — Campylobacter is the classic. The pattern is ascending, symmetrical, areflexic weakness with relatively preserved sensation. Albuminocytological dissociation in CSF is characteristic. The danger is silent respiratory failure: sats stay normal until the patient decompensates.
puzzles.management: Serial forced vital capacity — not oximetry. FVC below 20 ml/kg or falling means critical care and possible intubation. IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange; steroids do not work. VTE prophylaxis, autonomic monitoring for arrhythmia and BP swings, and early physiotherapy.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS / NHS England – Guillain-Barré syndrome

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 19-year-old female presents with vomiting, diarrhoea and muscle aches since last night.
hints: Housemates had a sickness bug last week, so she assumed she had caught it.
Feels dizzy standing. Severe aching in both thighs and shoulders.
Mid-period. Has been using tampons and thinks one may still be in place.
O/E: Temp 39.4, BP 78/40, HR 132. Diffuse red rash like sunburn, including palms and soles.
Conjunctivae injected, tongue bright red. Creatinine 210, platelets 82, ALT 160, CK 900.
puzzles.explanation: Superantigen-mediated toxin release, classically staphylococcal from a retained tampon, causing massive cytokine activation. Fever, hypotension, a diffuse macular erythroderma involving palms and soles, and multi-organ involvement define it. The GI prodrome makes it look like gastroenteritis, and desquamation of the hands and feet comes a week or two later, far too late to help.
puzzles.management: Remove the source — retained tampon or packing — immediately. Aggressive fluid resuscitation and vasopressors. IV antibiotics combining an anti-staphylococcal agent with clindamycin to suppress toxin production. Consider IV immunoglobulin in refractory disease. Critical care involvement.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Sepsis / UKHSA toxic shock guidance

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 44-year-old female presents with episodes of headache and palpitations.
hints: Episodes last 20 minutes, come from nowhere, then pass. Told previously these are panic attacks.
Drenching sweats during the attacks, and she goes pale rather than flushed.
Blood pressure has been erratic at reviews: 210/120 once, 128/76 today. Three drugs, still uncontrolled.
Lost 6 kg without trying. Family history of thyroid cancer in her father.
24-hour urinary metanephrines markedly raised. CT abdomen: 4 cm right adrenal mass.
puzzles.explanation: Catecholamine-secreting tumour of the adrenal medulla. The triad is episodic headache, sweating and palpitations, and the paroxysmal nature with normal readings in between means it is very often labelled anxiety. Pallor during attacks, rather than flushing, is a useful discriminator. Around a quarter are part of an inherited syndrome such as MEN2.
puzzles.management: Confirm biochemically with plasma or 24-hour urinary metanephrines, then image. Alpha blockade with phenoxybenzamine FIRST, and only add a beta blocker afterwards — beta blockade alone causes unopposed alpha stimulation and hypertensive crisis. Surgical resection once fully alpha-blocked. Genetic testing.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Hypertension / Endocrine Society guidance

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 58-year-old female presents feeling shivery and generally unwell since last night.
hints: No cough, no dysuria, no diarrhoea. Cannot point to anything specific.
Had her second cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer 10 days ago.
Took paracetamol at home for the shivering before coming in.
O/E: Temp 37.6, HR 108, BP 102/60. Chest clear, abdomen soft. PICC line site looks clean.
WCC 1.2, neutrophils 0.3, CRP 90, lactate 2.4.
puzzles.explanation: Sepsis in a patient with a neutrophil count below 0.5, most often 7–14 days after chemotherapy. There is frequently no localising sign and no impressive fever, because the inflammatory response needs neutrophils to produce it — and paracetamol taken at home masks what little there is. Any temperature above 38, or any unwellness, in a recently treated patient is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise.
puzzles.management: Empirical IV piperacillin-tazobactam within one hour of arrival — do not wait for the neutrophil count or cultures to return. Blood cultures peripherally and from every lumen of the line. Full septic screen, fluids, acute oncology referral. Do not delay for a chest X-ray.
puzzles.source: NICE CG151 – Neutropenic sepsis in cancer patients

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 81-year-old male found on his bathroom floor by a neighbour, thought to have been there overnight.
hints: Fully alert. No head injury and no chest pain. Says he simply could not get up.
Both legs ache badly and feel swollen and weak.
Passed a small amount of very dark urine in the department. Dipstick: blood 4+.
Microscopy shows no red cells despite the positive dipstick.
CK 42,000, K 6.4, creatinine 260 (baseline 90), calcium 1.9, phosphate raised.
puzzles.explanation: Muscle breakdown after prolonged immobility releases myoglobin, potassium and phosphate. Myoglobin cross-reacts with the urine dipstick for blood, so a strongly positive dip with no red cells on microscopy is the giveaway. The long lie is easy to record as a mechanical fall and dehydration and the CK never gets checked. Hyperkalaemia and AKI are the immediate threats.
puzzles.management: Aggressive IV crystalloid to maintain a high urine output. Treat hyperkalaemia and monitor with continuous ECG. Serial CK, U&Es and calcium — avoid giving calcium unless there are ECG changes, since it precipitates. Stop nephrotoxic drugs and statins. Renal replacement if refractory. Look for compartment syndrome and treat the cause of the fall.
puzzles.source: NICE NG148 – Acute kidney injury

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 76-year-old female presents from her care home, drowsy and off her food for a week.
hints: Staff say she has slept more each day and is now difficult to rouse.
Drinking constantly but eating almost nothing. Getting through several pads a day.
PMH: type 2 diabetes on gliclazide. Started prednisolone 2 weeks ago for polymyalgia.
O/E: dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, skin tenting. GCS 13. No focal neurology. Temp 37.1.
Glucose 48, Na 158, osmolality 340, ketones 0.6, pH 7.36, creatinine 210.
puzzles.explanation: Profound hyperglycaemia and dehydration without significant ketosis, because residual insulin is enough to suppress ketogenesis. It develops over days to weeks in older type 2 patients and presents as drowsiness or confusion, so it is routinely worked up as a UTI or delirium. Steroids are a common precipitant. Mortality is far higher than DKA.
puzzles.management: IV 0.9% saline is the priority — replace fluid before insulin, and expect a large deficit. Aim to lower osmolality slowly to avoid central pontine myelinolysis. Low-dose insulin only if glucose stops falling with fluid alone, or if ketones are significant. VTE prophylaxis, as thrombotic risk is very high. Treat the precipitant.
puzzles.source: JBDS / NICE NG28 – Type 2 diabetes in adults

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 47-year-old male presents with a severe headache that began 2 hours ago.
hints: Pain sits behind the eyes. Vomited twice. Neck feels slightly stiff.
Vision has gone blurred and he is now seeing double.
On questioning: 2 years of tiredness, reduced libido and clumsiness with peripheral vision.
O/E: right third nerve palsy. Bitemporal field defect to confrontation. BP 86/54.
CT head: no subarachnoid blood; hyperdense mass in the sella. Na 126, 9am cortisol 62.
puzzles.explanation: Haemorrhage or infarction into a pituitary adenoma. It mimics subarachnoid haemorrhage exactly — sudden headache, vomiting, meningism — but the CT shows no blood in the cisterns and the clues are the cavernous sinus cranial nerve palsies and a chiasmal field defect. The adenoma is often previously undiagnosed. Hypotension and hyponatraemia mean acute secondary adrenal insufficiency.
puzzles.management: IV hydrocortisone immediately — the adrenal insufficiency kills, not the mass. Fluid resuscitation, careful sodium correction. Urgent pituitary MRI, full anterior pituitary profile and formal visual fields. Endocrine and neurosurgical review; transsphenoidal decompression for deteriorating vision or consciousness.
puzzles.source: Society for Endocrinology – Pituitary apoplexy guidance

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 24-year-old male presents with 3 weeks of tiredness and a sore mouth.
hints: Gums bleed whenever he brushes. Two nosebleeds this week.
Bruising over both shins that he cannot account for.
Three throat and chest infections in the last month, each given antibiotics.
O/E: pale. Petechiae over both ankles. Gums swollen and overgrown. No lymphadenopathy.
Hb 78, platelets 18, WCC 46 with circulating blasts. Auer rods on the film.
puzzles.explanation: Clonal proliferation of myeloid blasts crowding out normal marrow, producing the triad of anaemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia. Each symptom alone looks trivial — tired, bruises easily, keeps getting infections — which is why it is often several GP visits in. Gum infiltration is characteristic of monocytic subtypes, and Auer rods are diagnostic of myeloid lineage.
puzzles.management: Urgent same-day haematology referral. FBC, film, coagulation screen, LDH, urate. Bone marrow aspirate with immunophenotyping and cytogenetics. Treat as neutropenic sepsis if febrile. Tumour lysis prophylaxis with hydration and allopurinol or rasburicase. Intensive chemotherapy; suspect APL and start ATRA if coagulopathy is present.
puzzles.source: NICE NG12 – Suspected cancer: recognition and referral

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 33-year-old male presents with 8 weeks of cough.
hints: Dry at first, now productive. Occasional streak of blood in the sputum.
Drenching night sweats, changing the sheets. 9 kg weight loss.
Moved to the UK from Pakistan 8 months ago. A housemate has a similar cough.
Two courses of amoxicillin from his GP with no improvement. No wheeze, no fever spikes.
CXR: right upper lobe cavitating consolidation. Sputum: acid-fast bacilli on microscopy.
puzzles.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis reactivating in the apical segments, where oxygen tension is highest. A cough lasting more than three weeks with weight loss and night sweats, unresponsive to standard antibiotics, should prompt the diagnosis. Migration from a high-incidence country and household contacts are the key risk factors. Haemoptysis is often minimal.
puzzles.management: Three sputum samples for smear, culture and NAAT. Airborne isolation in a negative-pressure side room. RIPE therapy: rifampicin and isoniazid for 6 months, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for the first 2, with pyridoxine. Notify public health, arrange contact tracing, and offer HIV testing. Monitor LFTs and warn about visual acuity on ethambutol.
puzzles.source: NICE NG33 – Tuberculosis

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 28-year-old female presents with 6 months of tiredness and bloating.
hints: Loose, pale, offensive stools that are difficult to flush.
Told previously she has IBS. Cutting out dairy made no difference.
Two courses of iron tablets, but the ferritin keeps falling. Periods are normal.
Itchy blistering rash over both elbows and the buttocks for the past year.
Hb 101, MCV 76, ferritin 6. Anti-tTG strongly positive with normal total IgA. Duodenal biopsy: villous atrophy.
puzzles.explanation: Immune reaction to gluten causing villous atrophy and malabsorption. Adults typically present with unexplained iron deficiency, fatigue and bloating rather than dramatic diarrhoea, so the IBS label sticks for years. Iron deficiency refractory to replacement, in a menstruating woman with normal periods, is the clue. The rash is dermatitis herpetiformis and is effectively diagnostic.
puzzles.management: Test anti-tTG IgA with total IgA WHILE still eating gluten — a gluten-free diet before testing invalidates it. Duodenal biopsy to confirm. Lifelong gluten-free diet with dietitian input. Check bone density, and vitamin and mineral levels. Pneumococcal vaccination because of functional hyposplenism. Annual review.
puzzles.source: NICE NG20 – Coeliac disease

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 4-year-old female brought in by her parents, pale and passing very little urine.
hints: Bloody diarrhoea last week which settled 3 days ago. She had seemed to be recovering.
Since then increasingly tired, and puffy around the eyes in the mornings.
The family visited an open farm 10 days ago and fed the lambs.
O/E: pale, periorbital oedema, BP 118/76. Abdomen soft. Alert but withdrawn.
Hb 68, platelets 42, creatinine 210. Film: fragmented red cells. Stool culture: E. coli O157.
puzzles.explanation: Shiga toxin from E. coli O157 damages endothelium, giving the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. The critical pattern is a child who improves after bloody diarrhoea and then deteriorates a few days later with pallor and reduced urine output. Farm visits and undercooked meat are typical exposures.
puzzles.management: Supportive care is the mainstay — careful fluid and electrolyte balance, treat hypertension, transfuse for symptomatic anaemia. Avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents, which increase toxin release. Avoid platelet transfusion unless bleeding. Renal replacement therapy if needed. Notify public health. Most children recover renal function.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Gastroenteritis in children / UKHSA STEC guidance

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 29-year-old female presents at 32 weeks pregnant with constant abdominal pain.
hints: Pain began an hour ago and does not ease off at all between tightenings.
Only a small amount of dark blood noticed on wiping. Feels the baby moving less.
Smokes 10 a day. Blood pressure has been running high at antenatal checks.
O/E: uterus firm and tender and does not relax. Fundus larger than expected for dates.
HR 116, BP 94/58, Hb 92. CTG: reduced variability with late decelerations.
puzzles.explanation: Premature separation of the placenta. Most of the blood is concealed behind the placenta, so visible bleeding is a poor guide to severity and the woman can be in shock with almost no external loss. A continuously hard, tender uterus distinguishes it from labour, and painless bleeding would suggest praevia instead. Hypertension and smoking are the main risk factors.
puzzles.management: A-E resuscitation, large-bore access, cross-match, activate major haemorrhage protocol if unstable. Continuous CTG. Do NOT perform a vaginal examination until praevia is excluded. Anti-D if rhesus negative, with a Kleihauer test. Urgent delivery — usually category 1 caesarean — for fetal compromise or maternal instability. Watch for DIC and postpartum haemorrhage.
puzzles.source: RCOG GTG 63 / NICE NG121 – Antenatal and intrapartum care

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 23-year-old female presents with 8 hours of right iliac fossa pain and vomiting.
hints: Pain came on abruptly while she was at the gym, and comes in severe waves.
No fever. Appetite was completely normal until the pain started.
Last period 2 weeks ago. Urine hCG negative. An ovarian cyst was noted on a scan last year.
O/E: tender right iliac fossa with guarding. Rovsing's sign negative. Temp 36.8, WCC 11.
Transvaginal ultrasound: 7 cm right adnexal mass, oedematous ovary, absent Doppler flow.
puzzles.explanation: The ovary twists on its pedicle, usually where an existing cyst gives it mass. It is the mimic of appendicitis in young women — but the onset is abrupt rather than gradual, the pain is colicky, appetite is preserved and there is little fever or leucocytosis. A pre-existing cyst and sudden movement are typical. Doppler flow can be preserved, so a normal scan does not exclude it.
puzzles.management: Urgent gynaecology referral. Exclude pregnancy in every case. Analgesia, nil by mouth. Diagnostic laparoscopy with detorsion, aiming to conserve the ovary even if it looks dusky — appearance is a poor guide to viability. Cystectomy at the same time or later. Oophorectomy only for clearly necrotic tissue.
puzzles.source: RCOG GTG 62 – Management of suspected ovarian masses

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 55-year-old male presents with 10 days of worsening mid-back pain.
hints: Pain is constant and worse at night. Lying still does not help.
Fevers and shaking chills for the past 3 days.
Injects heroin into the groin. Treated for cellulitis at an injection site last month.
O/E: Temp 38.6. Exquisite tenderness on percussing T8. Legs 4/5 with brisk reflexes.
WCC 20, CRP 280. Blood cultures: Staphylococcus aureus. MRI: epidural collection T7–T9.
puzzles.explanation: Pus collecting in the epidural space, usually haematogenous Staph aureus. The classic triad of back pain, fever and neurological deficit is complete in a minority, and the fever is often blamed on the injecting rather than the spine. Progression from root pain to weakness to paralysis can take hours. Injecting drug use, diabetes and recent bacteraemia are the risk factors.
puzzles.management: Urgent whole-spine MRI with contrast — the abscess is often multi-level. Blood cultures before antibiotics, then prolonged IV antimicrobials guided by culture, typically 6 weeks or more. Immediate neurosurgical referral for decompression and drainage if there is any neurological deficit. Echocardiogram to look for concurrent endocarditis.
puzzles.source: NICE NG59 – Low back pain and sciatica / BIA spinal infection guidance

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 48-year-old male presents with vomiting and upper abdominal discomfort since last night.
hints: Cannot keep anything down. Retching brings no relief.
The pain bores through to his back and is easier when he sits forward.
Large meal and heavy drinking at a wedding two nights ago. Gallstones noted on a scan last year.
O/E: epigastric tenderness with guarding. Bowel sounds reduced. Temp 37.8, HR 112.
Amylase 1,340. Calcium 1.94, glucose 13, LDH 480. CT: oedematous pancreas with peripancreatic fluid.
puzzles.explanation: Autodigestion of the pancreas, in the UK most often from gallstones or alcohol. Vomiting that does not relieve the pain, and pain radiating through to the back and eased by sitting forward, are the discriminators from gastritis. Severity is scored with Glasgow-Imrie or APACHE II, not by the amylase level — hypocalcaemia, hyperglycaemia and a raised LDH here all count towards a severe episode.
puzzles.management: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation, analgesia, antiemetics, catheter and strict fluid balance. Nil by mouth is not required — enteral feeding is preferred if tolerated. Score severity and consider HDU. Ultrasound for gallstones and check LFTs and triglycerides. ERCP if there is coexisting cholangitis. Cholecystectomy on the same admission for gallstone pancreatitis.
puzzles.source: NICE NG104 – Pancreatitis

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 62-year-old male presents with 3 months of right shoulder pain.
hints: Dull constant ache spreading into the inner arm. Six weeks of physiotherapy did nothing.
Ring and little fingers of the right hand feel numb and clumsy. Grip is weakening.
40 pack-year smoker. 8 kg weight loss. Occasional dry cough he blames on the smoking.
O/E: shoulder movements full and painless. Wasting of the small muscles of the right hand.
Right-sided ptosis with a constricted pupil and a dry face. CXR: right apical opacity.
puzzles.explanation: A tumour at the lung apex invading the brachial plexus and sympathetic chain — a Pancoast tumour. It presents to musculoskeletal and physiotherapy services as shoulder pain, and the chest is never examined. T1 root involvement gives lower brachial plexus wasting; sympathetic chain involvement gives Horner's syndrome of ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis. Apical shadowing is easily missed behind the clavicles on a plain film.
puzzles.management: Urgent two-week-wait chest X-ray and respiratory referral. Contrast CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging, then PET-CT and tissue biopsy. Treatment is usually concurrent chemoradiotherapy with consideration of surgical resection. Assess for spinal and vascular invasion. Analgesia is often neuropathic.
puzzles.source: NICE NG122 – Lung cancer: diagnosis and management

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 58-year-old male presents with 4 days of diarrhoea and feeling muddled.
hints: Family say he has been confused since yesterday. Headache and aching all over.
Dry cough started 2 days ago. High fevers, but he is not especially breathless.
Returned a week ago from a package holiday in Spain. Two others on the trip are unwell.
O/E: Temp 39.4 but HR only 92. Crackles at the right base. No neck stiffness.
Na 122, ALT 180, CRP 320. CXR: right lower lobe consolidation. Urinary antigen positive.
puzzles.explanation: Legionella pneumophila from contaminated water systems, classically air conditioning or hotel plumbing. The extrapulmonary features dominate — diarrhoea, confusion, myalgia — so it is worked up as gastroenteritis or delirium while the chest signs are minimal. Hyponatraemia, deranged LFTs and a relative bradycardia for the degree of fever are the biochemical fingerprints.
puzzles.management: CURB-65 to guide severity and setting. Legionella and pneumococcal urinary antigens. A macrolide or fluoroquinolone — beta-lactams alone will not cover it. Correct sodium slowly. Notifiable disease: inform public health so the water source can be traced and other travellers identified.
puzzles.source: NICE NG138 – Pneumonia in adults / BTS CAP guidance

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 2-year-old male brought in with a cough and wheeze lasting 3 weeks.
hints: Two courses of inhalers from the GP with no benefit at all. No fever.
Cough is worse at night. He has never wheezed before this episode.
Mother now recalls a choking and coughing fit at a family party 3 weeks ago while eating nuts.
O/E: wheeze audible only over the right chest. Left side clear. Chest looks asymmetrical.
Expiratory CXR: hyperinflated right lung with mediastinal shift to the left.
puzzles.explanation: An inhaled object lodges in the right main bronchus, which is wider and more vertical. The initial choking episode is often forgotten or not volunteered, and the child is then treated for asthma or recurrent viral wheeze for weeks. Persistently unilateral wheeze is the key sign — asthma is bilateral. Air trapping is best shown on an expiratory or lateral decubitus film, and a normal inspiratory film does not exclude it.
puzzles.management: Do not attempt blind finger sweeps. Keep the child calm and avoid distressing them. Urgent ENT or paediatric surgical referral for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthetic, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Antibiotics only if there is secondary infection or established collapse.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Cough in children / Resuscitation Council UK choking guidance

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 34-year-old female presents feeling fluey with a sore mouth and gritty eyes.
hints: Cannot eat — her lips and mouth are too painful. Ulcers inside both cheeks.
Stinging when passing urine. Both eyes red, sore and sticky.
Started lamotrigine for epilepsy 3 weeks ago. No other new medication.
O/E: dusky red target-like macules over the trunk, a few now blistering.
Skin shears away with gentle lateral pressure. Around 8% body surface involved. Temp 38.5.
puzzles.explanation: A severe delayed drug hypersensitivity causing keratinocyte apoptosis and epidermal detachment. The prodrome is a flu-like illness with mucosal pain, so it is sent home as a viral illness before the skin declares itself. Two or more mucosal surfaces involved is the giveaway. Detachment under 10% is Stevens-Johnson, over 30% is toxic epidermal necrolysis. Anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides and NSAIDs are the usual culprits.
puzzles.management: Stop the offending drug immediately and permanently. Transfer to a burns or dermatology unit. Supportive care dominates: fluid and electrolyte replacement, temperature control, analgesia, meticulous wound care and nutritional support. Urgent ophthalmology review to prevent scarring and blindness. Calculate SCORTEN. Avoid prophylactic antibiotics.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Drug allergy / BAD SJS-TEN guidelines

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 4-year-old male presents with a fever and pain around the left ear.
hints: Had earache 6 days ago. The GP prescribed amoxicillin and it seemed to settle.
The fever came back yesterday. He is miserable and off his food.
Mother says his left ear now sticks out more than the right one.
O/E: tender boggy swelling behind the left ear. Pinna pushed forward and downward.
Left tympanic membrane bulging and dull. Temp 39.1, WCC 19, CRP 160.
puzzles.explanation: Infection spreads from the middle ear into the mastoid air cells. It is the child who appeared to be recovering from otitis media and then relapses. Postauricular swelling with a protruding pinna is the defining sign — otitis media alone does not displace the ear. Complications include subperiosteal abscess, facial nerve palsy, sigmoid sinus thrombosis and intracranial extension.
puzzles.management: Admit for IV antibiotics and urgent ENT review. CT temporal bones if there is any suspicion of abscess or intracranial spread, or if there is no response within 24–48 hours. Myringotomy with grommet insertion for drainage; cortical mastoidectomy if there is an abscess or failure to improve.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Otitis media acute

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 7-year-old female presents with a swollen right eyelid.
hints: Swelling began yesterday and is markedly worse today. She is febrile and unhappy.
Heavy cold with a blocked nose for the past week.
Says it hurts to look around and is keeping the eye shut.
O/E: eyelid red and tense. The eye appears pushed forward. Upgaze painful and restricted.
Colour vision reduced on that side. CT sinuses: ethmoid sinusitis with a subperiosteal collection.
puzzles.explanation: Infection posterior to the orbital septum, usually spreading from the ethmoid sinuses. Preseptal cellulitis looks similar from the outside but the three features that separate them are pain on eye movement, restricted movement or proptosis, and reduced visual acuity or colour vision. Vision loss and cavernous sinus thrombosis follow if it is treated as a simple lid infection.
puzzles.management: Admit under joint ophthalmology and ENT care. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics without delay. Contrast CT of orbits and sinuses. Four-hourly visual acuity, colour vision and pupil checks. Surgical drainage of any abscess or for failure to improve. Nasal decongestants for the underlying sinusitis.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Preseptal and orbital cellulitis

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 5-year-old male presents with puffy eyes his mother assumed were an allergy.
hints: Swelling is worst first thing in the morning and eases a little through the day.
Antihistamines made no difference. No rash, no itching, no wheeze.
His tummy looks swollen and his shoes no longer fit. Off his food.
O/E: periorbital and ankle oedema, shifting dullness in the abdomen. BP normal, afebrile.
Urine dip: protein 4+, no blood. Albumin 16, cholesterol raised, creatinine normal.
puzzles.explanation: Heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema. Periorbital swelling worst on waking is repeatedly mistaken for allergy or insect bites, and the diagnosis is made on a urine dipstick that nobody performs. In children aged 2–10 it is minimal change disease in around 90% of cases, and a normal blood pressure with no haematuria supports that — features suggesting nephritic syndrome instead would be hypertension and blood on the dip.
puzzles.management: Confirm with early morning urine protein:creatinine ratio and albumin. Oral prednisolone without biopsy in typical childhood presentations. Biopsy only for atypical features, steroid resistance, or age outside 2–10. Fluid and salt restriction, monitor for the complications: infection from immunoglobulin loss, thrombosis, and hypovolaemia.
puzzles.source: NICE CKS – Nephrotic syndrome / RCPCH guidance

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 64-year-old female presents with 3 days of breathlessness and swollen ankles.
hints: Worse lying flat. Light-headed whenever she stands up.
Vague chest tightness for a fortnight. Treated for pericarditis a month ago.
PMH: breast cancer 3 years ago, discharged from follow-up last year.
O/E: JVP raised and rises further on inspiration. Heart sounds very quiet. Chest clear.
BP 92/68, falling to 74/60 on inspiration. ECG: small complexes with alternating amplitude.
puzzles.explanation: Pericardial fluid accumulating fast enough to prevent ventricular filling. Breathlessness with raised JVP and oedema reads as heart failure — but the lungs are clear, which they would not be in left ventricular failure. Beck's triad is hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds. A JVP that rises on inspiration is Kussmaul's sign, and a fall in systolic pressure over 10 mmHg on inspiration is pulsus paradoxus. Malignancy is a common cause.
puzzles.management: Urgent bedside echocardiography — do not wait for a formal scan. IV fluids to maintain preload while arranging definitive treatment. Avoid diuretics, vasodilators and positive pressure ventilation, all of which reduce filling and can precipitate arrest. Urgent pericardiocentesis, ideally echo-guided. Send fluid for cytology and culture.
puzzles.source: ESC – Pericardial diseases guidelines

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 22-year-old female presents with 5 days of lower abdominal pain and irregular bleeding.
hints: Treated for a urine infection last week, but the culture came back negative.
Bleeding between periods and after sex. Discharge has changed and smells different.
Deep pain during intercourse. New partner 2 months ago, condoms used inconsistently.
O/E: bilateral lower abdominal tenderness. Temp 37.9. Adnexal tenderness on bimanual.
Marked cervical excitation. Urine hCG negative. NAAT: Chlamydia trachomatis positive.
puzzles.explanation: Ascending infection of the upper genital tract, usually chlamydia or gonorrhoea. Symptoms are mild and non-specific, so it is treated as a urinary infection or period pain while tubal scarring accumulates — the sequelae are infertility, chronic pelvic pain and ectopic pregnancy. A negative urine culture in a young woman treated for UTI should prompt a sexual history. Always exclude pregnancy first, because ectopic is the dangerous mimic.
puzzles.management: Treat empirically on clinical suspicion; do not wait for swab results. Ceftriaxone with doxycycline and metronidazole. Take endocervical NAATs, offer a full sexual health screen including HIV, and arrange partner notification through GUM. Advise abstinence until both are treated. Remove an IUD only if no improvement. Admit if pregnant, septic, or a tubo-ovarian abscess is suspected.
puzzles.source: BASHH / NICE CKS – Pelvic inflammatory disease

puzzles.presentingComplaint: 84-year-old female presents with left groin pain after a fall two days ago.
hints: She got herself up afterwards and has been walking since, slowly and with a stick.
Pain sits in the groin and radiates to the knee. Worst standing up from a chair.
PMH: osteoporosis on alendronate. Two other falls this year. Lives alone.
O/E: leg not shortened, not externally rotated. Pain on axial loading and log-roll.
AP and lateral hip X-rays reported as normal. MRI hip: undisplaced intracapsular fracture.
puzzles.explanation: An impacted or undisplaced fracture retains enough stability to allow weight bearing, and shows no shortening or external rotation — so the classic picture is entirely absent. Around 2–10% are not visible on the initial plain film. Pain referred to the knee via the obturator nerve adds to the confusion. Sending the patient home risks displacement and avascular necrosis.
puzzles.management: If clinical suspicion persists despite normal X-rays, obtain MRI within 24 hours — CT if MRI is unavailable or contraindicated. Analgesia including a fascia iliaca block, and orthogeriatric input from admission. Surgery within 36 hours: internal fixation for undisplaced intracapsular fractures in fitter patients. Falls and bone health assessment before discharge.
puzzles.source: NICE CG124 – Hip fracture: management
